rw: This clause makes timely performance a material term, so a late delivery or completion can count as a breach and let the other party cancel or claim damages.

ww.The contract has no price set out anywhe: That describes a missing price term, which is a different gap in a contract and has nothing to do with deadlines or the timing of performance.
ww.The contract lasts forever and can never: A contract does not last forever because of this phrase, and the phrase says nothing about duration; it concerns the importance of meeting the stated deadlines.
ww.Deadlines are optional and late work is: The phrase means the opposite: deadlines are strict, so late performance is not automatically acceptable and may expose the late party to liability for breach.

rw: A time is of the essence clause makes the date a material term, so arriving June 13 for a June 12 wedding is a clear breach allowing cancellation and damages.

ww.Choice of law clause: A choice of law clause only picks which state's law governs the contract, so it says nothing about a caterer who arrives a day late.
ww.Severability clause: A severability clause keeps the rest of a contract alive if one provision is struck down, and it has no bearing on missed dates or deadlines.
ww.Force majeure clause: Force majeure excuses performance for events beyond a party's control, such as storms, and a caterer simply arriving a day late would not usually qualify.

rw: Force majeure, French for superior force, frees a party from liability when events such as natural disasters, war or government orders make performance impossible or impractical.

ww.A clause that doubles the price if the g: A holiday price increase would be an ordinary pricing term; force majeure is not about changing prices but about excusing performance after unforeseeable outside events.
ww.A clause that assigns ownership of the g: Transferring ownership of goods is handled by title and delivery terms, not by force majeure, which concerns excuses for events like floods, wars or strikes.
ww.A clause that adds interest to late paym: Interest on late payments is a separate financial term in a contract; force majeure does not add charges but relieves a party of duties in extraordinary events.

rw: A general partnership is owned by two or more people who share profits and management, and each partner is personally liable without limit for the firm's debts.

ww.A government agency that regulates the t: That describes a federal regulatory body, not a business; a general partnership is a private business formed by owners and it does not set taxes or regulate trade.
ww.A business owned by shareholders with li: That describes a corporation, where shareholders own the company and their personal assets are protected, unlike partners in a general partnership who face unlimited liability.
ww.A business with a single owner who keeps: That describes a sole proprietorship, which has just one owner; a partnership by definition requires at least two owners who share profits, control and risk.

rw: Each partner is an agent of the partnership, so a contract made within the ordinary course of business binds the partnership even if the other partner was never told.

ww.Only Partner B is bound: Partner B did not sign or know of the deal, and a partnership contract does not bind only the partner who stayed uninvolved; the firm itself is bound.
ww.No one at all is bound: The contract is valid and enforceable against the partnership because the supplier dealt with an agent acting within normal business, so someone is clearly bound.
ww.Only Partner A is bound: Partner A is personally liable too, but the contract does not stop there; the partnership and so all partners are bound since A acted within normal business.

rw: A C corporation pays corporate income tax on its profits, and shareholders then pay personal tax on dividends paid from what is left, so the same earnings are taxed twice.

ww.Profits are taxed twice at the same rate: Corporate profits are taxed at the corporate rate and later as shareholder dividends; double taxation is not about the state and nation both taxing at the same rate.
ww.Employees pay taxes twice on their wages: Wages are taxed once as employee income; double taxation concerns corporate profits taxed at the company level and again when distributed, not an employee's pay being taxed twice.
ww.Shareholders are taxed twice, once on th: Shareholders are not taxed on salaries as part of double taxation; the second tax falls on dividends paid out of profits that the corporation already paid tax on.

rw: A pass-through entity, such as an LLC, partnership or S corporation, pays no entity-level income tax; profits and losses pass to owners who report them on personal returns.

ww.A business owned by a state government a: A state-owned enterprise is government property and says nothing about how taxes flow; pass-through status concerns owners reporting profits on personal returns, not public ownership.
ww.A business that pays no taxes ever, what: Pass-through entities still generate taxable income for their owners; the profits are taxed once on personal returns, so the claim of paying no taxes at all is false.
ww.A business taxed twice, once as a firm a: That is a C corporation, which is taxed on profits at the corporate level and again on dividends; a pass-through entity avoids this second layer of tax.

rw: An LLC protects owners' personal assets from business debts and by default passes profits through to the owners' personal returns, combining both features.

ww.Sole owner: A sole proprietorship has pass-through taxation but the owner has unlimited personal liability for business debts, so it lacks the liability protection the question requires.
ww.C corp: A C corporation gives owners limited liability but its profits face double taxation, so it does not offer pass-through treatment as the question asks.
ww.A GP firm: A general partnership has pass-through taxation, but each partner faces unlimited personal liability for the firm's debts, so it fails the limited liability requirement.

rw: A corporation is owned by its shareholders, who hold shares of stock and elect the board of directors to oversee the business on their behalf.

ww.Its employees: Employees work for the corporation and may hold stock, but employment alone gives no ownership; ownership comes only from holding shares of the company's stock.
ww.Its customers: Customers buy the corporation's products and services but have no ownership claim on the company unless they separately buy its shares as investors.
ww.Its suppliers: Suppliers sell materials and services to the corporation as business partners, but supplying goods creates no ownership; only holding shares of stock does.

rw: Shareholders elect directors to oversee the corporation, set major policy, appoint senior officers and protect shareholder interests, while officers handle day-to-day operations of the business.

ww.A group of employees chosen by managers: Managers answer to the board, not the reverse; directors are elected by shareholders rather than chosen by managers, and they oversee the firm instead of running daily operations.
ww.A group of lenders that fund the firm wi: Lenders are creditors who are repaid under loan terms; they do not form the board, which is elected by shareholders to oversee the corporation.
ww.A group of customers who vote on the fir: Customers do not vote on major decisions; the board is elected by shareholders, who are the owners, and it guides the corporation on their behalf.

rw: Officers and directors owe a fiduciary duty of loyalty, which requires putting the corporation's interests ahead of their own, so a self-serving sale at its expense violates it.

ww.The duty to advertise the sale: Advertising has nothing to do with the officer's self-dealing; the problem is putting personal gain ahead of the corporation, not a missing promotional duty.
ww.The duty to hire more staff: Hiring staff is an operational choice and unrelated to the conflict of interest; the officer's wrong lies in favoring a personal company over the corporation.
ww.The duty to audit the books: Auditing books relates to financial controls and oversight, not to the self-dealing here, where the officer put personal interests ahead of the corporation's.

rw: Courts may pierce the corporate veil and hold owners personally liable when they commingle funds, ignore formalities, undercapitalize the firm or use it to commit fraud.

ww.Raising capital by selling new shares of: Selling new shares to the public is an initial or secondary public offering, a way to raise capital, and has nothing to do with disregarding corporate limited liability.
ww.Protecting owners from all liability in: Piercing the veil is the opposite of protecting owners from all liability; it is the exception where courts remove that protection when owners abuse the corporate form.
ww.Merging two companies into one larger fi: Combining two companies is a merger or acquisition and does not involve piercing the veil, which concerns removing owners' limited liability protection after abuse.

rw: A franchise agreement lets the franchisee operate under the franchisor's brand, trademarks and business system in exchange for fees and royalties, subject to standards and control.

ww.A loan agreement between a bank and a bu: A bank loan is a financing contract that creates debt; a franchise agreement is about licensing a brand and system rather than lending money to a business owner.
ww.A contract to buy stock in a company fro: Buying stock transfers a share of company ownership, while a franchise gives only the right to use a brand and system, not ownership of the franchisor.
ww.A lease for land only, with no brand or: A franchise includes the brand and operating system, so a plain land lease with neither does not qualify as a franchise agreement.

rw: Franchise agreements require uniform menus, quality and branding so customers get the same experience everywhere, so the franchisor can object when a franchisee changes the menu alone.

ww.Menus are not part of the business under: Menus are generally part of the business and its brand standards, which the agreement controls, so claiming they fall outside the agreement is not a sound reason.
ww.Franchise law forbids all menus from bei: Franchise law does not forbid all menu changes; it is the franchise contract and brand standards that restrict changes without approval, and approved changes are allowed.
ww.Franchisees own the trademark and the br: The franchisor owns the trademark and brand name and licenses them to the franchisee, who does not own them, which is why the franchisor can enforce standards.

rw: A limited partner invests capital, shares in profits and risks losing only the amount invested, but cannot take part in management without risking losing that limited liability.

ww.A creditor of the firm who lent money to: That describes a creditor, who lends money and is repaid under loan terms; a limited partner is an owner-investor who shares profits rather than a lender.
ww.A person who owns no part of the firm an: A limited partner does own part of the firm and shares in its profits, so a person with no ownership or profit right would not be a partner.
ww.A partner with unlimited liability who m: That describes a general partner, who manages the firm and has unlimited personal liability; a limited partner has capped liability and no management role.

rw: An operating agreement sets out how an LLC is managed, each member's ownership share, voting rights, how profits and losses are divided and what happens when members leave.

ww.How products are shipped to customers ea: Shipping logistics are day-to-day operations handled by managers and are not the subject of an operating agreement, which sets internal rules for owners.
ww.How customers pay for goods and services: Customer payment methods are business operations and sales policy, not governance; the operating agreement covers owners' rights, management structure and profit sharing in the LLC.
ww.How taxes are filed by customers who buy: Customers file their own taxes; an operating agreement governs the LLC's internal affairs among members and has nothing to do with tax filings by buyers.

rw: Articles of incorporation, filed with the state, create the corporation as a separate legal entity and set out basics such as its name, purpose, registered agent and authorized shares.

ww.A trademark application form: A trademark application protects a brand name or logo with the federal trademark office and does not create a corporation or give it legal existence.
ww.A warranty card for buyers: A warranty card records a product guarantee for buyers and has no role in forming a corporation, which requires a filing with the state.
ww.An invoice for the goods: An invoice is a bill for goods sold, a routine business document, and plays no part in creating a corporation as a legal entity.

rw: Apparent authority arises when a principal's words or conduct lead a third party to reasonably believe an agent is authorized, so the principal may be bound even without actual permission.

ww.Authority held by a court of law over th: That describes jurisdiction, a court's power over a case and its parties, which is a procedural concept and not a form of authority held by an agent.
ww.No authority at all to act for anyone in: Apparent authority is not the absence of authority; it is the appearance of authority created by the principal, which can bind the principal to contracts the agent signs.
ww.Authority written in a contract only, ne: That describes express authority, which can be written, while apparent authority comes from the principal's conduct and need not be written anywhere in a contract.

rw: Letting the clerk wear a manager's badge made the supplier reasonably believe the clerk had authority, so the store may be bound by apparent authority even without actual permission.

ww.The supplier must pay the store, as the: The clerk's lack of leave to sign does not release the supplier or the store; the supplier is entitled to rely on appearances, and the supplier would not owe the store payment.
ww.No contract is possible with the store o: A contract is possible here because the store's conduct gave the clerk the look of authority, so the claim that no contract can exist with the store is wrong.
ww.Only the clerk is bound by the supply co: The clerk acted as an agent for the store, so the store can be bound rather than only the clerk, because the store's own conduct created the appearance of authority.

rw: The principal is the person who authorizes an agent to act on their behalf, and the principal is bound by the agent's actions within that authority.

ww.The person who inspects the agent's work: An inspector or supervisor checks work quality but does not authorize the agent; the principal is the person on whose behalf, and with whose authority, the agent acts.
ww.The person who drafts the agent's contra: Drafting a contract is a lawyer's or manager's task; the principal is defined by authorizing the agent to act for them, not by writing the agent's contract.
ww.The school leader in charge of the staff: In agency law the principal is not a school head; the word here means the party who gives an agent authority to act for them in dealings with third parties.

rw: When a company controls hours and how the work is done, the worker is likely an employee, because the right to control the manner of work is the key test.

ww.She uses her own tools and sets her own: Using her own tools, setting her own schedule and working for many clients are marks of an independent contractor, not an employee, because she controls the work.
ww.She works for several clients at the sam: Serving several clients at once suggests independence and a contractor relationship, since employees usually work for one employer who controls their time and work.
ww.She sends invoices for each project and: Sending invoices and paying her own taxes are typical of independent contractors, while employers withhold taxes and pay employees through payroll.

rw: Under respondeat superior an employer can be liable for torts committed by an employee within the scope of employment, and the driver is also personally liable for the crash.

ww.Only the other driver is paid: The other driver is not the only party who matters; the question asks who may be liable for the crash, and payment of the other driver is not a legal rule.
ww.Only the police are liable: Police do not become liable for a delivery crash; liability falls on the people who caused the harm, here the driver and the employer under agency law.
ww.No one is liable at all: A crash that causes harm can create liability, so saying no one is liable ignores negligence law and the employer's responsibility for employees acting within their job.

rw: At-will employment lets either the employer or the employee end the relationship at any time, with or without notice, so long as the reason is not illegal.

ww.Employment that always needs a reason an: At-will employment does not need any reason and does not need a court order to end; requiring cause is what a contract or union agreement typically provides.
ww.Employment with no pay for the person wh: At-will describes the right to end the job and says nothing about pay; employees under it are still entitled to lawful wages for the work done.
ww.Employment for a fixed term agreed by bo: A fixed term is the opposite of at-will employment, where either side may end the job at any time and no set length of service is promised.

rw: Firing someone soon after they report safety violations suggests retaliation, which laws such as OSHA and whistleblower statutes prohibit, and the close timing supports that claim.

ww.Trade dilution: Trade dilution is a trademark concept about weakening a famous brand, so it has no relevance to firing a worker who reported safety problems to a government agency.
ww.Price fixing: Price fixing is an antitrust violation where competitors agree on prices, which has nothing to do with discipline or termination after an employee's safety report.
ww.Breach of terms: Breach of terms relates to contract duties, but the facts here, a firing right after a protected safety report, point most directly to a retaliation claim instead.

rw: Real property includes land and anything permanently attached to it, such as buildings, trees and fixtures, together with the rights that come with owning them.

ww.Stock certificates and bonds held by inv: Stocks and bonds are personal property, specifically intangible financial assets, because they are not land and are not permanently attached to land.
ww.Furniture and other movable household it: Furniture and movable household items are personal property since they can be moved and are not permanently attached to land or buildings.
ww.A car, a truck or any other motor vehicl: Vehicles are movable and so count as personal property, even though they are valuable; they are not land or permanent fixtures.

rw: Personal property is anything movable and not attached to land, such as vehicles, equipment, furniture and inventory, as opposed to land and permanent fixtures.

ww.Mineral rights beneath land, real proper: Mineral rights beneath land are interests in real property, because they belong to the land itself and are not movable items.
ww.A permanent building on a piece of land: A permanent building on land is real property, since it is attached to the land and not movable like personal property.
ww.Land, houses and other fixed objects on: Land, houses and fixed objects on land are all real property, the opposite of personal property, which consists of movable items.

rw: A movable bookshelf is personal property and not a fixture, so it stays the tenant's and the tenant may remove it when moving out.

ww.The landlord, because it is real propert: A movable bookshelf is not attached to the building, so it is not real property, and the landlord has no claim to it based on that label.
ww.No one may keep it after the tenant move: The tenant may keep the bookshelf at move-out; the claim that no one may keep it has no basis in property law for a movable item.
ww.The bank, because it holds the tenant's: A bank holding a lease has no ownership of a tenant's movable furniture; leases give rights to use the premises, not title to the tenant's belongings.

rw: A lease is a contract in which an owner gives another party the right to use property for a set time, usually in exchange for rent, while keeping ownership.

ww.A contract to buy property permanently f: That describes a purchase agreement, which transfers ownership permanently; a lease only gives the right to use property for a limited time in exchange for rent.
ww.A loan on property from a bank, repaid i: A loan on property from a bank is a mortgage, which is a financing agreement; a lease is a contract between a landlord and a tenant.
ww.A tax on property paid by the owner to t: A tax paid on property to local government is a property tax, a levy and not a contract; a lease is an agreement between landlord and tenant.

rw: Eminent domain lets the government take private property for public use, such as roads or schools, as long as the owner receives just compensation under the Fifth Amendment.

ww.A buyer's right to cancel a purchase wit: A right to cancel a purchase within days of buying a home describes a rescission or cooling-off right, not eminent domain, which is a government power.
ww.A landlord's right to evict a tenant who: A landlord's right to evict a nonpaying tenant is an eviction remedy under landlord-tenant law and has no connection to the government's eminent domain power.
ww.A bank's right to foreclose on a home wh: A bank's right to foreclose on a home after nonpayment is a lender's remedy under a mortgage, while eminent domain is the government's power to take property.

rw: The Fifth Amendment requires just compensation, meaning fair market value, when the government takes private property for public use, such as a new road.

ww.Nothing at all: The Constitution does not allow the government to take property for nothing; the Takings Clause requires fair payment to the owner, so offering nothing at all is wrong.
ww.A permit to build: A building permit allows construction and is not payment for land taken; the owner is entitled to just compensation, not a permit for a new project.
ww.A tax credit only: A tax credit alone does not satisfy the Takings Clause, which requires just compensation, usually fair market value paid in money for the land taken.

rw: An intentional tort is a civil wrong committed on purpose, such as assault, battery, false imprisonment or defamation, where the person meant to act, and it can bring damages.

ww.A tax dispute between a firm and the rev: A tax dispute between a firm and the revenue agency is an administrative or tax law matter, not a tort, which is a civil wrong that harms another person.
ww.A contract breach by one side that fails: A contract breach is a failure to perform a promise, which is a separate area of law from torts, which are wrongs that do not depend on a contract.
ww.A careless act with no intent to cause h: Careless acts without intent to harm are negligence, not intentional torts, because an intentional tort requires that the wrongdoer meant to commit the act.

rw: Defamation is a false statement of fact that harms someone's reputation; a knowing false public accusation of theft is a classic example of this intentional tort.

ww.Trespass: Trespass is unauthorized entry onto someone's land and has nothing to do with a false public accusation of theft made about an employee.
ww.Negligence: Negligence involves carelessness, but here the manager knowingly made a false statement, so the better fit is the intentional tort of defamation rather than negligence.
ww.Conversion: Conversion is the wrongful taking or use of another's property and does not describe a false statement harming an employee's reputation.

rw: Strict product liability holds sellers and manufacturers liable for injuries from defective, unreasonably dangerous products without the plaintiff proving negligence, only that a defect caused harm.

ww.Statute of frauds rule: The statute of frauds requires certain contracts to be in writing and has no bearing on a claim for injury caused by a defective product.
ww.Liquidated damages term: Liquidated damages is a contract term that fixes damages in advance, not a basis for a claim by an injured user against a seller.
ww.Adverse possession of land: Adverse possession is a way to gain title to land by long, open use, and has nothing to do with injuries from defective products.

rw: Copyright protects original works of authorship fixed in a tangible form, such as books, music, art and software, and arises automatically when the work is created.

ww.Protection for trade secrets such as rec: Trade secrets such as recipes and formulas are protected by trade secret law, which depends on keeping them confidential, not by copyright protection.
ww.Protection for brand names, logos and sl: Brand names, logos and slogans are protected by trademark law, not copyright, which protects creative expression rather than words used to identify a source of goods.
ww.Protection for inventions such as new ma: Inventions such as machines and processes are protected by patents, which require an application, while copyright covers expressive works instead of functional inventions.

rw: Fair use permits limited use of copyrighted material without permission for purposes like criticism, commentary, news reporting, teaching and research, judged by four factors.

ww.Renting copyrighted work to other people: Renting copyrighted work to others for a fee without permission is not fair use; it would infringe the owner's rights, which include control over distribution.
ww.Copying any work for free, forever, what: Fair use does not allow copying any work for free forever; it is a limited defense that courts weigh by factors, regardless of what creators say.
ww.Unlimited copying for profit, with no cr: Unlimited copying for profit without credit is infringement; fair use is limited, and commercial copying of a whole work weighs strongly against it.

rw: Copying a whole popular song for a commercial ad weighs against fair use on the purpose, amount used and market effect factors, so it likely infringes.

ww.Yes, because it is advertising and ads m: Advertising is commercial use, and ads cannot freely use any song; using music in an ad without permission usually requires a license from the copyright holder.
ww.Yes, because it was short and only a par: The question states the business copied the entire song, so the claim that it was short and only a part contradicts the facts and weakens the fair use argument.
ww.Yes, because songs are public property a: Songs are protected by copyright and are not public property, so using one in an ad without permission generally requires a license from the owner.

rw: A trademark can last indefinitely as long as the owner keeps using it in commerce and files the required maintenance renewals with the trademark office.

ww.Exactly 20 years from the filing: Twenty years is the term of a utility patent from filing, not a trademark, which can last as long as it is used and renewed.
ww.Until the owner retires or sells up: Trademark rights do not end when the owner retires or sells; they can be sold with the business and continue as long as the mark is used.
ww.One year only, then it must end: A trademark is not limited to one year; protection continues as long as the mark remains in use and the owner makes required renewals.

rw: UCC Article 2 governs contracts for the sale of goods, meaning movable tangible items, and it covers formation, warranties, delivery, risk of loss and remedies for breach.

ww.The sale of land: The sale of land is governed by real property law, not the UCC, which covers movable goods and not interests in real estate.
ww.Tax filing rules: Tax filing rules are found in tax law, not the UCC, which is a uniform set of state commercial laws.
ww.Employment rules: Employment rules are found in labor and employment statutes, not in the UCC, which regulates commercial transactions like sales of goods.

rw: The UCC statute of frauds requires a signed writing for sales of goods priced at $500 or more under the original code, and a writing is generally required to enforce larger sales.

ww.Notarized by a public notary: Notarization is not required for goods contracts; a signed writing is what the UCC statute of frauds asks for, not a notary public's certificate.
ww.Oral only, with no writing: An oral-only agreement for goods at this price generally cannot be enforced under the statute of frauds, so a contract resting on no writing is the weak choice here.
ww.Recorded on video and stored: Video recording does not satisfy the writing requirement and is not required; the law asks for a signed written record showing the contract's key terms.

rw: An implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose arises when a seller knows the buyer's special need and the buyer relies on the seller's advice to select suitable goods.

ww.Merchantability, for ordinary use: Merchantability is a general warranty that goods are fit for ordinary use, but here the buyer told the seller a specific need, which points to a different warranty.
ww.No warranty applies to the sale: Implied warranties arise automatically in sales unless properly disclaimed, so saying that no warranty applies ignores the clerk's recommendation after the buyer stated her need.
ww.Title to the goods being sold: The warranty of title promises the seller owns the goods and can transfer them; it does not address whether the mattress suits the buyer's back problem.

rw: Lemon laws give buyers of new vehicles with substantial defects that the maker cannot fix after reasonable attempts a remedy such as a refund or replacement.

ww.A law on car insurance that sets minimum: Car insurance minimums are set by separate state insurance laws, not by lemon laws, which protect buyers of defective vehicles rather than set insurance cover.
ww.A law on sales tax charged in each state: Sales tax is a separate state revenue law, whereas lemon laws deal with defective vehicles rather than taxes charged to shoppers.
ww.A law about fruit sold in stores and sol: Despite the name, a lemon law has nothing to do with fruit sales and instead protects consumers who buy defective new cars from the manufacturer.

rw: TILA requires lenders to disclose the cost of credit, including the annual percentage rate and finance charges, in a standard form so consumers can compare offers.

ww.Lenders to waive all interest on their l: The Truth in Lending Act does not require interest waivers; it requires clear disclosure of credit terms so borrowers can compare loan costs.
ww.Banks to lend to everyone who asks for a: TILA does not force banks to lend to everyone; lenders may still decide whom to approve, subject to other laws against discrimination.
ww.Borrowers to repay within 24 hours of th: TILA does not require repayment within 24 hours; it concerns disclosure of loan terms, and repayment schedules are set by the loan contract.

rw: The Truth in Lending Act requires lenders to disclose the APR and other credit costs clearly, so hiding a high APR behind a low payment ad implicates it.

ww.The Sherman Act of 1890: The Sherman Act of 1890 is an antitrust law against monopolies and price fixing and does not address disclosure of loan costs.
ww.The Fair Labor Standards Act: The Fair Labor Standards Act sets minimum wage and overtime rules for workers and does not regulate how lenders advertise loan costs.
ww.The Clean Air Act of 1970: The Clean Air Act of 1970 addresses air pollution and environmental standards and has nothing to do with loan advertising or disclosure.

rw: The FCRA promotes the accuracy, fairness and privacy of consumer credit information held by credit bureaus and gives consumers the right to see and dispute their reports.

ww.Stock prices set on the major exchanges: Stock prices are set by trading and overseen by securities laws, not by the Fair Credit Reporting Act, which concerns consumer credit reports.
ww.Business tax rates set by the state and: Business tax rates are set by tax law and legislatures, not the Fair Credit Reporting Act, which covers how credit information is collected and used.
ww.Interest rates on savings, as offered by: Savings interest rates are set by banks and market conditions; the FCRA is about credit report accuracy and privacy rather than rates on deposits.

rw: The FDCPA bans abusive, deceptive and harassing debt collection practices, such as repeated threatening calls, false statements and contact at inconvenient times or places.

ww.Opening a savings account at a bank with: Opening a savings account is a normal banking activity and is not prohibited by any law, much less the debt collection law.
ww.Paying debts on time and in full each mo: Paying debts on time is encouraged and legal; the FDCPA restricts how collectors behave, not how consumers pay what they owe.
ww.Any debt repayment plan made between a d: The FDCPA does not forbid repayment plans; voluntary arrangements between debtor and creditor are common and lawful, while the law targets collectors' abusive tactics.

rw: Calling a consumer at work after being told to stop and threatening arrest are practices the FDCPA bans, so this is a likely violation of the law.

ww.A credit report update sent to the borro: A credit report update is a bureau action and not a collector's phone call, so it does not describe the harassing conduct in the question.
ww.A normal collection step in the process: Debt collection law limits what collectors may do, and calling a workplace after a request to stop plus threatening arrest is not a normal permitted step.
ww.A required notice about the debt owed: A validation notice is a written statement about the debt that collectors must send; threatening arrest by phone at work is not such a notice.

rw: The FTC rule lets buyers cancel certain door-to-door and off-premises sales of $25 or more within three business days, helping them escape high-pressure sales.

ww.Buyers must wait a year before they can: The Cooling-Off Rule gives buyers three days to cancel, not a year, and a year-long wait would defeat its purpose of protecting against pressure sales.
ww.Sellers can cancel at any time, whatever: The rule protects buyers, not sellers; a seller cannot cancel whenever it likes after making a promise, since that would undermine the sale contract.
ww.Buyers must pay twice for each sale made: The rule does not require double payment; it gives buyers a right to cancel and get a refund, and it does not add costs to buyers.

rw: Under UCC Article 3 a negotiable instrument must be a signed writing with an unconditional promise or order to pay a fixed amount of money, payable on demand or at a definite time.

ww.It must promise services only, never mon: A negotiable instrument must be a written promise or order to pay money, not services, and it cannot be merely spoken aloud as a verbal promise.
ww.It must be unsigned and may be left blan: A negotiable instrument must be signed by the maker or drawer, so an unsigned and blank instrument fails the UCC Article 3 requirements.
ww.It must be spoken aloud before two witne: Negotiable instruments must be in writing under the UCC, so an oral promise made before witnesses cannot qualify as a negotiable instrument.

rw: Endorsement is the payee signing the back of a check, which lets the payee transfer it to another person or deposit it at a bank.

ww.Printing the front of the check with the: Printing on the front of the check with the amount is filling in the check by the drawer, not endorsement, which happens on the back by the payee.
ww.Raising the amount shown on the check: Raising the amount is alteration, a form of forgery that is illegal, and has no connection to the lawful act of endorsing a check.
ww.Voiding the check and then tearing it up: Voiding and tearing up a check cancels it, whereas endorsement is a signature on the back that allows transfer or deposit.

rw: A signature alone on the back is a blank endorsement, making the check payable to the bearer, so anyone who finds it may be able to cash or deposit it.

ww.It cannot be lost or stolen by anyone: Checks can be lost or stolen like any other item, so claiming that no one can take it ignores the risk created by a blank endorsement.
ww.Only the employer can cash it as it name: A paycheck names the worker as payee, not the employer, so the employer cannot cash it; the risk comes from the worker's own signature on the back.
ww.It is automatically void and worthless: Losing a signed check does not void it; the check stays valid, and the employer can stop payment and reissue it if the worker acts quickly.

rw: Perfection is the set of steps, usually filing a financing statement or taking possession of the collateral, that make a security interest effective against other creditors.

ww.Making a product perfect so that it meet: Perfection is a legal term from secured transactions and has nothing to do with product quality standards set by makers and buyers.
ww.Cancelling a loan so that the borrower n: Cancelling a loan is a release or discharge of debt, whereas perfection is the step a lender takes to make its security interest effective against third parties.
ww.Paying a debt early so that the lender c: Paying a debt early is prepayment of the loan, a borrower's act, and not a lender's step to protect a security interest in collateral.

rw: Under UCC priority rules, the secured party who first files or perfects generally has priority in the collateral over later claimants, so the earlier perfected lender wins.

ww.The lender who lent last of all: Lending last gives a lender no advantage; priority generally goes to whoever perfected first, and a later lender usually ranks behind earlier perfected ones.
ww.The lender with the larger loan: The size of the loan does not decide priority; the order of filing or perfection controls, so a larger loan gives no better claim by itself.
ww.Neither lender has any claim: Both lenders may have valid security interests, so neither lacking a claim is wrong; priority rules decide which one is paid first from the collateral.

rw: The FLSA is the federal law that sets the minimum wage, overtime pay at one and a half times the regular rate over 40 hours a week, and child labor limits.

ww.A law on imports and duties on goods com: Imports and duties on foreign goods are covered by customs and tariff laws, not the FLSA, which regulates pay and working conditions for workers.
ww.A law on stock sales and share prices on: Stock sales and share prices are regulated by securities laws such as the Securities Exchange Act, not by the FLSA, which concerns wages and hours.
ww.A law on trademarks and brand names used: Trademarks and brand names are protected under the Lanham Act, and the FLSA addresses minimum wage, overtime and child labor instead.

rw: The first 40 hours pay 40 times $20, or $800. The 6 overtime hours pay 1.5 times $20, or $30 each, for $180. The total is $980.

ww.$800: $800 equals only 40 hours at $20 and ignores the 6 overtime hours, which must be paid at least one and a half times the regular rate.
ww.$1,100: $1,100 overstates the pay; the correct total is 40 times $20 plus 6 overtime hours at $30, which comes to less than $1,100.
ww.$920: $920 is 46 hours times $20 at the straight rate, but the FLSA requires time and a half for the 6 hours over 40, so the minimum is higher.

rw: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibits employers from discriminating in hiring, firing, pay and conditions because of race, color, religion, sex or national origin.

ww.A law on retirement accounts and the pen: Retirement accounts and pensions are governed by ERISA, not Title VII, which is a civil rights law about discrimination in employment.
ww.A law on workplace safety standards and: Workplace safety standards come from OSHA, not Title VII, which deals with discrimination and not factory inspections.
ww.A law on minimum wage rates and the pay: Minimum wage and hourly pay come from the Fair Labor Standards Act, while Title VII prohibits discrimination based on protected characteristics.

rw: The ADA requires employers to provide reasonable accommodations to qualified employees with disabilities, such as modified equipment or schedules, unless doing so causes undue hardship.

ww.Hire staff without holding any interview: The ADA does not ban interviews or tests; employers may use job-related screening, though they cannot discriminate against qualified people because of a disability.
ww.Pay everyone the same wage whatever thei: The ADA does not require equal pay for all jobs; it prohibits discrimination and requires accommodation rather than setting identical wages for everyone.
ww.Ignore disabilities when the job tasks a: The ADA does not tell employers to ignore disabilities; it requires considering reasonable accommodations so qualified people can perform the essential functions of the job.

rw: The ADA requires employers to consider and provide reasonable accommodations, such as an adjustable desk, unless they can show that doing so would create undue hardship.

ww.Fire the employee because she asked for: Firing an employee for asking for an accommodation is unlawful discrimination and retaliation under the ADA, so it is never the right response.
ww.Deny the request because the desk is far: An employer cannot simply deny the request by calling it costly; a lower desk is a modest accommodation, and denial requires proof of undue hardship.
ww.Ignore the request until someone else ra: Ignoring the request fails the interactive process the ADA expects, in which employer and employee discuss a possible accommodation promptly and in good faith.

rw: The FMLA lets eligible employees take up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave a year for family and medical reasons, such as a newborn or serious illness.

ww.A law on pensions and the retirement pla: Pensions and retirement plans fall under ERISA, not the FMLA, which provides leave rather than retirement benefits.
ww.A law banning all leave for workers who: The FMLA does not ban leave; it does the opposite by guaranteeing eligible workers time off for illness or the birth of a child.
ww.A law giving paid vacation to all worker: The FMLA leave is unpaid, not paid, and it does not grant vacation; paid vacation is a matter of employer policy rather than this law.

rw: The FMLA requires restoring a returning employee to the same or an equivalent position with the same pay, benefits and working conditions.

ww.Fire her a few days after her return fro: Firing an employee after FMLA leave would violate the law, which protects the job, so the employer cannot end her employment for taking leave.
ww.Demote her to a lower role after her ret: Demoting her after leave would be interference with FMLA rights, since the law requires return to the same or an equivalent role.
ww.Reduce her pay by half for the weeks she: FMLA leave is unpaid and cannot be penalized by a pay cut; returning employees must get equivalent pay, benefits and terms, not half pay.

rw: Form I-9 is completed by employers and new hires to verify identity and authorization to work in the United States, with supporting documents examined within three business days.

ww.Applying for a license to work in a regu: Work licenses for regulated fields are issued by state boards, not through Form I-9, which employers use to check identity and work eligibility.
ww.Reporting wages and tax withheld to the: Wages and tax withheld are reported on payroll tax forms such as Form 941 and W-2, not on Form I-9, which concerns work eligibility.
ww.Setting the rate of tax withholding on e: Withholding rates are set through Form W-4, which the employee fills in, while Form I-9 verifies identity and employment eligibility instead.

rw: Under the National Labor Relations Act, most employees have a protected right to discuss wages and working conditions, so discouraging such talk may be unlawful.

ww.Only managers may speak about pay with o: The law does not limit pay discussions to managers; most nonsupervisory employees have a protected right to talk about wages with coworkers.
ww.Employees may never discuss pay, since w: Wages are not secret by law, and employees generally may discuss pay, so a rule forbidding all pay talk creates the legal concern here.
ww.Pay is always secret by law in every sta: Pay is not automatically secret by law; many states and the NLRA protect pay discussions, so a blanket secrecy rule can violate employee rights.

rw: The Securities Act of 1933 requires companies selling securities to the public for the first time to register them and disclose accurate financial information to investors.

ww.To regulate shipping routes and ports us: Shipping routes and ports are governed by maritime and transport law, not the Securities Act of 1933, which deals with securities offerings.
ww.To ban stock trading by all firms and al: The Act does not ban stock trading; it regulates new offerings through disclosure, while trading in existing shares continues and is regulated by other laws.
ww.To set the minimum wage for all of the w: Minimum wage is set by the Fair Labor Standards Act and has nothing to do with the Securities Act of 1933 and its disclosure rules.

rw: The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 regulates trading of securities on the secondary market and created the Securities and Exchange Commission to enforce the securities laws.

ww.Sets interest on mortgages and fixes len: Mortgage rates are not set by the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, which regulates securities trading, brokers and exchanges.
ww.Regulates farm prices and the sale of cr: Farm prices and crop sales are covered by agricultural law, whereas the 1934 Act regulates trading in securities on exchanges.
ww.Regulates imports and the duties paid at: Imports and border duties are governed by customs and trade law, and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 concerns securities markets.

rw: Trading on material nonpublic information, like secret merger news, is insider trading, which the Securities Exchange Act and SEC Rule 10b-5 prohibit and punish.

ww.Antidiscrimination laws that protect wor: Antidiscrimination laws protect workers from unfair treatment and do not address trading on confidential merger news learned as an executive.
ww.Zoning laws about the use of land in cit: Zoning laws control how land is used in cities and have nothing to do with trading stocks on confidential information.
ww.Child labor laws about work by minors: Child labor laws limit work by minors, so they are unrelated to an executive using confidential merger news to buy stock early.

rw: A bankruptcy trustee is appointed to collect and manage the debtor's assets and distribute proceeds to creditors according to bankruptcy law.

ww.A judge who presides over the bankruptcy: The judge presides over the case and issues rulings, while the trustee is a separate administrator who handles the debtor's estate and payments to creditors.
ww.A debtor's friend who offers to lend the: A trustee is a neutral court-supervised officer, not the debtor's friend, and does not lend the debtor money in times of need.
ww.A tax collector who works for the revenu: A tax collector works for a revenue agency, whereas a bankruptcy trustee administers the debtor's estate on behalf of the court and the creditors.

rw: Chapter 7 liquidates nonexempt assets to pay creditors and then discharges many debts, while Chapter 13 lets an individual with regular income keep property and repay under a three to five year plan.

ww.Chapter 7 is for businesses only, and Ch: Both chapters are available to individuals; Chapter 7 is not limited to businesses and Chapter 13 is limited to individuals with regular income, not all people.
ww.They are identical in every respect and: The two chapters differ greatly: one liquidates assets while the other reorganizes debts through a plan, so they are not identical beyond the name.
ww.Chapter 13 erases all debt immediately,: This reverses the chapters: Chapter 13 does not erase debts immediately but requires a repayment plan, while Chapter 7 liquidates assets and discharges eligible debts.

rw: Chapter 13 lets an individual with a steady income keep her property, such as a house, while repaying debts under a court-approved plan lasting three to five years.

ww.Chapter 7: Chapter 7 liquidates nonexempt assets and could put her house at risk, and it does not provide a multiyear repayment plan.
ww.Chapter 11: Chapter 11 is a reorganization used mainly by businesses with complex finances, and it is too costly and complex for an individual repaying debts over five years.
ww.No such plan: A plan like this does exist: Chapter 13 provides exactly this arrangement for individuals with regular income who wish to keep their home while repaying debts.

rw: Tax avoidance is the lawful reduction of taxes using deductions, credits, retirement plans and other legal strategies that the tax code allows.

ww.Hiding income from the tax agency to pay: Hiding income from the tax agency is tax evasion, which is illegal, not tax avoidance, which remains within the law.
ww.Falsifying records to reduce the tax a p: Falsifying records to cut a tax bill is fraud and tax evasion, a crime that can bring fines and prison, unlike lawful avoidance.
ww.Not filing a return at all for several y: Failing to file for years is unlawful noncompliance, with penalties and possible prosecution, rather than a legal strategy to reduce taxes.

rw: Deliberately hiding cash sales from the IRS to pay less tax is tax evasion, a federal crime involving fraud that can lead to penalties and prison.

ww.A deduction: A deduction is a lawful reduction of taxable income for allowed expenses; hiding cash sales is not a deduction but an unlawful omission of income.
ww.Tax avoidance: Tax avoidance is lawful planning that reduces taxes within the rules, whereas concealing $50,000 of income is illegal and not avoidance.
ww.A tax credit: A tax credit directly reduces tax owed for qualifying items, so it is a lawful benefit and not the concealment of income described here.

rw: An embargo is a government ban on trade with a specific country, here imports, usually for political reasons, and it can be a form of sanction.

ww.Subsidy: A subsidy is government financial support for a business or industry, not a ban on trade with another country.
ww.Merger: A merger combines two companies into one, which has nothing to do with a government banning imports from a country.
ww.Tax cut: A tax cut lowers taxes for people or businesses, so it is not a trade ban on goods from a specific country.

rw: The World Trade Organization sets rules for trade between nations, runs trade negotiations and helps settle disputes among its member countries.

ww.Sets national tax rates and collects inc: National tax rates are set by governments and legislatures, not by the WTO, which deals with international trade rules between member countries.
ww.Prints currency and coins for use across: Printing currency and coins is done by national governments and central banks, and the WTO has no role in making money.
ww.Runs world airlines and sets the fares t: The WTO does not run airlines or set fares; airlines are private or state firms, and the WTO focuses on trade rules among countries.

rw: The FCPA is a U.S. law that makes it illegal for U.S. companies and individuals to bribe foreign officials to win or keep business, and it requires accurate accounting records.

ww.A law on tariffs and duties on goods cro: Tariffs and duties are governed by customs and trade laws, not the FCPA, which targets bribery of foreign officials.
ww.A law that bans exports to foreign state: Export controls and licensing are covered by separate export laws, while the FCPA concerns improper payments to foreign government officials.
ww.A law on minimum wage for workers in fac: Minimum wage is set by the Fair Labor Standards Act, so it is unrelated to the FCPA, which deals with international corruption.

rw: The FCPA prohibits U.S. companies from paying foreign officials to gain business advantages, and paying to speed up a permit may violate it unless it is a narrow routine facilitation payment.

ww.The ADA: The ADA protects people with disabilities and does not address payments to foreign officials, so it is not the law violated here.
ww.The CAA: The CAA, the Clean Air Act, concerns pollution and air quality, so it does not apply to a payment made to a foreign official.
ww.The FLSA: The FLSA sets wage and hour standards for workers and has no connection to payments to foreign officials for permits.

rw: Incoterms like FOB and CIF state who pays for freight and insurance and when risk of loss passes from seller to buyer, avoiding disputes in international sales.

ww.To set tax rates for all of the exporter: Shipping terms do not set tax rates; governments set taxes and customs duties, whereas FOB and CIF allocate cost and risk between buyer and seller.
ww.To avoid contracts with buyers in all ot: Exporters use shipping terms to define duties within a sale, not to avoid foreign buyers, and they help make international contracts clearer.
ww.To eliminate shipping costs for the buye: Shipping terms do not eliminate costs; they only decide who pays freight and insurance, so some party still bears these shipping expenses.

rw: In civil cases the plaintiff must show the claim is more likely true than not, called a preponderance of the evidence, which is a lower standard than in criminal cases.

ww.A unanimous vote of the public: Civil cases are decided by a judge or jury applying a legal standard, not by a public vote, which has no place in court.
ww.A signed confession by the party: A confession by the defendant is not required in a civil case, and plaintiffs usually prove claims with evidence, testimony and documents instead.
ww.Proof beyond any reasonable doubt: Beyond a reasonable doubt is the higher standard used in criminal cases, whereas civil plaintiffs only need to meet a lower burden.

rw: Precedent is a prior court decision that courts follow when deciding later cases with similar facts, under the doctrine of stare decisis, which promotes consistency.

ww.A contract term fixing the price of good: Fixing the price of goods is a contract term and not a precedent, which is a legal principle from earlier court rulings.
ww.A new law from Congress that ends past r: A new law from Congress is a statute, and it may change court rules, but it is not a precedent set by earlier court decisions.
ww.A tax rule applied to the sale of goods: Tax rules on the sale of goods are set by statutes and regulations, not by precedent, which is based on earlier judicial opinions.

rw: A statute is a written law passed by a legislature, such as Congress or a state legislature, and it applies to the public within its jurisdiction.

ww.A company policy on staff pay: A company policy on pay is an internal rule set by an employer, not a statute, which is a law passed by a government legislature.
ww.A private contract by two parties: A private contract between two parties binds only those parties and is not a statute, which is a public law made by a legislature.
ww.A judge's written opinion: A judge's written opinion is case law, which applies and interprets statutes, but it is not itself a statute passed by a legislature.

rw: Under the Supremacy Clause of the Constitution, valid federal law overrides conflicting state law, so the federal law generally prevails when the two conflict.

ww.The older law: The age of a law does not decide a conflict between federal and state law; the Supremacy Clause says federal law takes priority regardless of date.
ww.The state law: The state law does not win a conflict with a valid federal law on the same subject, because the Supremacy Clause makes federal law supreme.
ww.Neither law: One of the laws does prevail; the Supremacy Clause establishes that valid federal law controls over conflicting state law, so neither law winning is wrong.

rw: The plaintiff is the party who starts a lawsuit by filing a complaint, bringing a claim against the defendant and seeking a remedy such as damages.

ww.Defends against the claim in court: The party who defends against the claim in court is the defendant, not the plaintiff, who is the person who starts the case.
ww.Writes the statute for the whole court: Statutes are written by legislatures, not by plaintiffs, who only bring a case to court asking for a remedy.
ww.Decides the case for both of the parties: The judge or jury decides the case, not the plaintiff, who is simply one of the parties asking the court to decide.

rw: Small claims courts handle disputes involving limited amounts of money, with simple procedures and often no lawyers, so ordinary people can resolve minor claims quickly and cheaply.

ww.Federal crimes tried before a jury of tw: Federal crimes are tried in federal district courts, often before juries, and small claims courts do not hear criminal cases.
ww.Constitutional appeals heard by the high: Constitutional appeals go to appellate courts and ultimately the Supreme Court, not small claims courts that handle minor money disputes.
ww.Billion-dollar mergers between large com: Billion-dollar mergers involve large complex transactions that belong in regulatory review or major courts, not small claims courts with low dollar limits.

rw: Knowingly selling a defective, unsafe product to meet quotas puts profit over safety and is unethical and likely illegal, exposing the firm to product liability.

ww.A required legal practice by firms: No law requires selling a product known to be defective; selling one is a legal risk, not a required practice for firms.
ww.Good salesmanship by the seller: Good salesmanship is honest and does not hide dangers, so knowingly selling a defective product is deceptive rather than skilled selling.
ww.A neutral business choice by the seller: Selling a known unsafe product is not neutral, because it risks harming customers and breaches duties of honesty and safety that businesses owe.

rw: Corporate social responsibility is a company's commitment to act ethically and to benefit society and the environment, beyond simply maximizing profit or following the law.

ww.A legal requirement for every product so: Corporate social responsibility is generally voluntary, not a legal requirement for every product, even though some laws do impose specific obligations.
ww.A sales tactic used only by the largest: CSR is practiced by firms of all sizes, not only the largest retailers, and it is a business approach rather than only a sales tactic.
ww.A tax loophole used by large firms to cu: CSR is not a tax loophole; it concerns ethical and social commitments, while tax loopholes are legal gaps used to reduce a tax bill.

rw: Strong business ethics go beyond legality, so choosing the option that benefits the community, even if both are legal, shows responsibility toward stakeholders.

ww.The cheaper option always: Always choosing the cheaper option puts cost above community welfare, and it does not reflect strong ethics when a beneficial legal option exists.
ww.Neither option works: Refusing both options is not reasonable here, because a legal and beneficial option exists and a company can choose it to act ethically.
ww.The harmful legal option: Choosing a legal but harmful option puts profit ahead of the community, so it meets the law but fails the test of strong ethics.

rw: Transparency builds customer trust and loyalty and reduces the risk of deception or false advertising claims by giving customers accurate information.

ww.It increases secrecy and cuts trust amon: Transparency reduces secrecy and builds trust, so saying it increases secrecy and cuts trust among staff reverses its actual effect.
ww.It lowers quality and weakens the loyalt: Transparency tends to raise trust and loyalty rather than lower quality or weaken customer loyalty, because honest dealing strengthens relationships.
ww.It avoids all laws and all rules in ever: Transparency does not let companies avoid laws; businesses must follow all applicable laws, and being open with customers is simply good practice.

rw: An accountant should decline to backdate the document and report the request to a supervisor, compliance officer or authority, because honesty and professional standards come first.

ww.Backdate it to keep the job: Backdating a document to look compliant is fraud and an ethical breach, and keeping a job is no excuse for falsifying records.
ww.Wait and see what happens next: Waiting and doing nothing allows a falsified record to stand and leaves the accountant exposed to professional and legal consequences.
ww.Backdate it but tell no one: Backdating secretly is still falsification, and hiding it makes the accountant complicit in fraud, which violates professional ethics and the law.

rw: The parol evidence rule bars evidence of prior oral agreements that contradict or add to a fully integrated written contract, so the court will likely exclude the oral promise.

ww.Void the entire contract automatically,: A merger clause does not void the contract; it states the writing is the complete agreement, which is why earlier oral promises are usually excluded.
ww.Add the oral promise to the contract as: Adding the oral promise would defeat the merger clause and the parol evidence rule, which keep earlier oral terms out of a final written agreement.
ww.Require the parties to restart negotiati: Courts enforce the written agreement as is, so they do not usually send the parties back to renegotiate when a merger clause covers the whole deal.

rw: Anticipatory repudiation occurs when a party clearly states or shows before performance is due that it will not perform, allowing the other side to treat it as a breach.

ww.Assigning the contract to someone else,: Assigning a contract transfers rights or duties to another person, which is different from refusing in advance to perform the contract.
ww.Asking to renegotiate the terms of the c: Politely asking to renegotiate is not repudiation, because the party has not clearly stated that it will not perform its obligations.
ww.Performing the contract early, before th: Early performance is not repudiation, because the party is carrying out its duties rather than refusing to perform them.

rw: Because the builder clearly repudiated in March, the homeowner may treat it as a breach now, hire another builder and seek damages for any extra cost.

ww.Sue for the builder's profits only, in c: The homeowner's remedy is not limited to the builder's profits; she may recover damages for the breach, such as extra cost to hire a replacement builder.
ww.Wait silently until June, then ask for a: She need not wait silently until June, because after a clear repudiation the other party may treat the contract as breached right away and mitigate damages.
ww.Do nothing because no breach occurred ye: A breach can occur before the due date through anticipatory repudiation, so the claim that no breach has happened yet at all is wrong.

rw: Substantial performance means the party has met the essential purpose of the contract despite minor defects, so the other side must pay, less the cost of fixing the flaws.

ww.Doing exactly what was promised in every: Doing everything exactly is perfect or full performance, which is stricter than substantial performance, where minor flaws are tolerated.
ww.Delaying a decade before starting the wo: Waiting a decade to start work is a material delay and does not meet the essential purpose, so it is not substantial performance.
ww.Doing none of the work that the contract: Doing none of the work is total nonperformance and a breach, which is the opposite of substantial performance.

rw: Substantial performance lets the painter recover the contract price minus the cost of repairing the small unfinished defect, which balances both sides' interests.

ww.No payment at all for the work done on t: Under substantial performance the painter who finished nearly all of the job can still be paid, so no payment at all would be unfair.
ww.Cancellation of all duties, so no one ow: One minor defect does not cancel all duties; substantial performance keeps the contract alive, so the owner must still pay after the deduction.
ww.Double payment for the work done on the: Double payment would give the painter more than the contract price, while substantial performance gives full price less a deduction for the defect.

rw: In an accord and satisfaction the parties agree to accept different performance (the accord) in place of the original duty, and carrying it out (the satisfaction) discharges the duty.

ww.A contract that is never signed by the p: A contract that is never signed does not describe an accord and satisfaction, which is an agreement to substitute performance, not an invalid agreement.
ww.A court order that forces one side to pa: A court order requiring payment for harm describes a judgment awarding damages, not an accord and satisfaction, which parties create by agreement themselves.
ww.A contract with no terms at all, written: A contract with no terms and just a signature has no content, whereas an accord and satisfaction has a clear substitute performance that both sides accept.

rw: A novation replaces an original party or contract with a new one, with the consent of all parties, and releases the original party from its obligations.

ww.A contract signed by one party only, whi: A contract binding the other side without its consent is invalid, whereas a novation requires the consent of everyone involved.
ww.A late fee charged by a landlord when th: A late fee is a penalty on rent paid after the due date and has nothing to do with replacing a party to a contract.
ww.A written warning sent by an employer to: A written warning from an employer to a late worker is discipline and not a novation, which changes the parties or terms of a contract.

rw: A novation substitutes a new party for the original one with everyone's agreement and releases the original supplier from the contract, as the facts describe.

ww.A rescission: Rescission cancels a contract and returns the parties to their positions before it, but here a new company takes over the duties, which is a different arrangement.
ww.A breach: A breach is a failure to perform, whereas here the parties agreed to a substitution, so nothing was breached.
ww.An assignment: An assignment transfers rights but usually does not release the original party from liability; the release of the original supplier points to a novation.

rw: The duty to mitigate requires the injured party to take reasonable steps to avoid or reduce its losses after a breach, and damages may be reduced if it fails to do so.

ww.The injured party must increase its loss: The duty to mitigate is the opposite of increasing losses; the injured party must act reasonably to reduce them, not raise them to inflate a claim.
ww.The breaching party must pay double the: The duty to mitigate rests on the injured party, not the breaching party, and it does not require anyone to pay double damages.
ww.The court must reduce all claims brought: Courts do not cut all claims by default; the duty to mitigate limits recovery only for losses that the injured party could reasonably have avoided.

rw: A landlord must make reasonable efforts to re-rent after a tenant leaves early, so leaving the unit empty for a year without trying can limit recovery under the duty to mitigate.

ww.The statute of frauds rule: The statute of frauds concerns whether certain contracts must be in writing, not whether the landlord tried to reduce its losses by re-renting.
ww.The parol evidence rule here: The parol evidence rule limits use of earlier oral statements to change a written contract, so it does not address the landlord's failure to re-rent.
ww.Respondeat superior doctrine: Respondeat superior makes employers liable for employees' acts, so it has nothing to do with a landlord's duty to reduce losses after a tenant leaves.

rw: An unconscionable contract is so one-sided and unfair, often because of unequal bargaining power, that a court may refuse to enforce it or strike the offending terms.

ww.A contract with a low price agreed by bo: A low price agreed by both parties is not unconscionable on its own; courts look for gross unfairness and lack of real choice, not just a low price.
ww.A contract that is long and has a great: Length and the number of pages do not make a contract unconscionable; courts look at fairness and bargaining power, not how long the document is.
ww.A contract signed on Monday that cannot: Signing on a particular day and being unable to change terms later describes an ordinary binding contract, not an unconscionable one.

rw: A contract of adhesion is a standardized form drafted by the stronger party and offered take-it-or-leave-it, with the other party unable to negotiate, and courts may scrutinize it closely.

ww.A negotiated deal between equals, where: A negotiated deal between equals is the opposite of an adhesion contract, which offers the weaker party no chance to bargain over terms.
ww.A contract made orally only, with no wri: Oral contracts are valid in many cases but have nothing to do with adhesion, which concerns a standard form drafted by one party and imposed on the other.
ww.A contract signed by sticking notes onto: Sticking notes onto a document is not how contracts are formed, and adhesion refers to unequal bargaining power rather than the physical way a document is signed.

rw: A term letting a company change any term at any time without notice is very one-sided, so a court may find it unconscionable or unenforceable in part.

ww.Void because it is printed in small type: Small print on the back does not void a contract by itself; the concern here is the unfairly one-sided power to change any term without notice.
ww.A gift that the company gives to every c: A service contract is not a gift, because customers pay for the service, and the issue is whether the one-sided change terms are fair.
ww.Always enforceable, since customers agre: Contracts are not always enforceable just because customers agree, because courts may refuse to enforce terms that are unconscionable or illusory, such as unlimited unilateral changes.

rw: A click-wrap agreement is an online contract that a user accepts by clicking I agree or a similar button, and courts generally enforce it when terms are clearly presented.

ww.A contract with no terms, only a blank p: A contract with no terms and a blank page lacks content, whereas a click-wrap agreement presents actual terms that a user accepts online.
ww.A contract written on paper only and sig: Paper contracts signed with a pen are traditional agreements, whereas a click-wrap agreement is formed electronically when a user clicks to accept.
ww.A contract made only by phone, with no w: Phone-only contracts are oral agreements, and click-wrap involves an online click on a written set of terms, so they are not the same.

rw: The E-SIGN Act of 2000 gives electronic signatures and records the same legal effect as paper and handwritten ones in many transactions, supporting online contracts.

ww.Requires every contract to be notarized: The E-SIGN Act does not require notarization; it makes electronic signatures and records valid, and many contracts do not need a notary.
ww.Bans electronic signatures on any contra: The E-SIGN Act does the opposite of banning electronic signatures; it recognizes them as legally valid for most contracts across the states.
ww.Sets interest rates that banks may charg: Interest rates on consumer loans are regulated by lending and usury laws, not by E-SIGN, which concerns the validity of electronic signatures.
